| [LIT-540](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-540.md) | Impulsive action: emotional impulses and their control | Frijda, Ridderinkhof & Rietveld (2014), Frontiers in Psychology 5:518. Impulsive action is non-deliberate but purposive. Automatic appraisal of an event's pertinence to the agent's concerns elicits a state of action readiness, a motive to establish, modify or end a relation to the object, with "control precedence" (urgency, persistence, attentional capture). Modes of action readiness are what distinguish one emotion from another. Events usually draw several appraisals and so several states of readiness, and their interaction regulates action: much emotion regulation is itself emotional, not reason overriding passion. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-433](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-433.md)); filed in place of Frijda's The Emotions ([LIT-546](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-546.md)), which could not be read, as the shortest lawfully readable statement of his action-readiness theory in his own words. Appraisal of an event's pertinence to one's concerns elicits a state of action readiness, a motive to change one's relation to the object, which has "control precedence". Modes of action readiness correspond to emotions (hostility to anger, avoidance to fear). Much emotion regulation is itself one state of action readiness checking another, so "there is no clear distinction between processes of emotion and processes of emotion regulation". It is a theoretical paper with no data, written for impulsive action, so it states the theory's core and not its full range. |

| [LIT-577](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-577.md) | Sophisticated Inference | Friston, Da Costa, Hafner, Hesp & Parr (2021; arXiv 2020), Neural Computation 33(3):713–763. Ordinary active inference scores a fixed set of policies by expected free energy (risk plus ambiguity). Sophisticated inference instead evaluates the expected free energy of the next action recursively, averaging over the beliefs the agent would hold after each plausible outcome and action, which amounts to a tree search over belief states pruned below a probability of 1/16. In simulations it plans past short-term costs: a rat visits a mildly aversive cue, and a horizon of four escapes a local minimum in a maze. It recovers Bayes-adaptive RL in the zero-temperature limit. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-454](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-454.md)), from the arXiv preprint, whose displayed equations did not survive text extraction. Worth reading as the active-inference planning scheme the record's free-energy holdings otherwise lack: expected free energy evaluated recursively over future belief states, a deep tree search pruned by probability, with the Bellman equation as its formal analogue. The evidence is small simulations (a T-maze rat and an 8 × 8 grid). In the "Dead Sea salt" experiment a lever that had predicted a disgusting salt solution became, on first presentation after a novel sodium appetite was induced and before any salt was retasted, nearly as attractive as a sucrose lever, with mesolimbic activation. | [LIT-585](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-585.md) | The Expected Value of Control: An Integrative Theory of Anterior Cingulate Cortex Function | Shenhav, Botvinick & Cohen (2013), Neuron 79(2):217-240. Worth reading as the standard statement that cognitive control is allocated by a cost-benefit decision. The "expected value of control" (EVC) of a control signal, which has an identity (which task) and an intensity (how much), is its expected payoff minus an intrinsic cost that rises with intensity. Dorsal anterior cingulate cortex is proposed to monitor and to specify the EVC-maximizing signal, which lateral PFC and subcortical structures then implement. It is a review and synthesis: the model is stated, not fitted, and the authors say the ingredients are not new. |
| [LIT-586](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-586.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Ainslie (2005), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 28(5), the précis of Breakdown of Will (2001). People and other animals discount delayed rewards hyperbolically, so preferences reverse as a smaller, sooner reward comes near, and a person becomes a population of reward-seeking "interests" that must forestall one another. Willpower is the bundling of future choices by treating the present one as a precedent: an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma, not an organ or a top-down ego. The same recursion predicts the will's costs: legalism, circumscribed "lapse districts", motivated blindness to lapses, and rules that favour countable goals over subtle ones. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md)), as the substitute for the 2001 book ([LIT-583](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-583.md)), which the owner suggested and which the précis follows chapter by chapter. Worth reading as the shortest complete statement of picoeconomics in Ainslie's own words. Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse as a smaller, sooner reward draws near, so a person behaves like a population of "interests" that bargain across time. Will is not a faculty above them but a recursive self-prediction: treating each choice as a precedent "bundles" future rewards, an intertemporal repeated prisoner's dilemma in which "credibility is power". The same mechanism predicts the will's side effects: legalism, "lapse districts", motivated misperception and compulsive over-control. |

| [LIT-1187](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1187.md) v2 | The construction of preference. | Slovic (1995), a review from an award address. Normatively equivalent elicitation procedures give systematically different preference orderings: in the Las Vegas study the two bets were chosen about equally often but the high-payoff bet was priced higher about 88% of the time, and Tversky, Slovic and Kahneman found 40–50% reversal rates of which 90% violated procedure invariance and 10% were intransitive. Scale compatibility and prominence explain the reversals. Slovic concludes that for important, complex and unfamiliar options preferences are "constructed on the spot" in elicitation. The evidence compares procedures; none follows a constructed preference into a later judgement. | Active — read 2026-10-16 ([NOTE-949](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-949.md)) in full, from a scan of the published article on a University of Florida course page, compared with the author's manuscript in the University of Oregon's ScholarsBank; worth reading as the compact review of preference reversals: normatively equivalent procedures give different orderings, about 90% of reversals violate procedure invariance rather than transitivity, and scale compatibility and prominence explain them. A typology of emotion theories in psychology (evolutionary, network, appraisal, goal-directed, psychological constructionist, social) and philosophy (feeling, judgmental, quasi-judgmental, perceptual, embodied, motivational), compared with tools from the philosophy of science. | [LIT-1434](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1434.md) | The power of goal-directed processes in the causation of emotional and other actions | Moors, Boddez & De Houwer (2017), Emotion Review 9(4):310–318. Standard dual-process models make stimulus-driven processes the default and give goal-directed ones a late, regulatory role, in action research and in emotion research alike. The authors reverse the default. Goal-directed processes, which select the action option with the highest expected utility, can be fast and automatic too, so most of the competition that decides behaviour is between goal-directed processes, settled by the values and expectancies of outcomes. Emotional action tendencies can be caused this way. Appraisal-to-action-tendency links are sophisticated stimulus-driven processes. Evidence for stimulus-driven control rests on null results open to hidden goals. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1117](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1117.md)): in full, from the submitted manuscript deposited in Ghent University's repository. Worth reading as the shortest statement of Moors's goal-directed account of emotional action, and as the nearest prior statement of the record's reading of appraisal as negotiation. Goal-directed processes, which weigh the utility of action options by the values and expectancies of their outcomes, are the default cause of action, emotional action included. Most of the competition that decides behaviour is between goal-directed processes, and its winner is fixed by values and expectancies. Control precedence is what high goal relevance produces, so an emotional episode is a decision process with higher stakes. The competition is run on a common currency, expected utility, which is the point where the record parts from it. |

| [LIT-1449](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1449.md) | Control Theory, Goal Attainment, and Psychopathology | Carver (2018), Psychological Inquiry 29(3):139–144, a commentary on DeYoung and Krueger. Problems arise wherever a feedback loop's input, reference value, comparison or output is extreme or biased. The five factors are read as sensitivities to classes of goals, not as loop parameters. | [LIT-1457](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1457.md) | The Emotion Process: Event Appraisal and Component Differentiation | Scherer & Moors (2019), Annual Review of Psychology 70:719–745. A review of experimental evidence on the emotion process, organised by five appraisal criteria (novelty, intrinsic and extrinsic valence, agency, control or power, fairness) and three paths from appraisal: to action tendencies, to physiological responses and to facial, vocal and gestural expression. Appraisal criteria have more stable response correlates than emotion categories do. Proposes that coherence among components above a threshold marks an episode, and above a second threshold awareness. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1106](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1106.md)): in full, from the PDF Annual Reviews serves to guest readers. Worth reading as the latest review of the component process model's evidence, organised by appraisal criterion rather than by emotion category. Its paths run from appraisal to action tendencies, to physiological responses and to expression. It separates intrinsic valence from goal congruence and reports the few studies that pull them apart: they have partly different physiological signatures and combine multiplicatively. It ends with a two-threshold proposal: coherence among components above one threshold starts an episode, and above a second it becomes aware. It does not describe appraisal as a negotiation among perspectives. |
| [LIT-1458](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1458.md) | Levels of valence | Shuman, Sander & Scherer (2013), Frontiers in Psychology 4:261. Valence exists at two levels. Micro-valences are the valenced outcomes of separate appraisal checks (pleasantness, goal conduciveness, power, self-congruence, moral goodness), and they can conflict, which explains mixed feelings. Macro-valence is one-dimensional, always present, and the common currency for choice. It is integrated from micro-valences and other inputs by rules ranging from weighted sums to lexicographic and elimination-by-aspects strategies. Intrinsic pleasantness and goal conduciveness are dissociable, citing Berridge. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1108](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1108.md)): in full, from the publisher's open-access PDF (Frontiers, CC licence). Worth reading as the component process model's own statement that valence is several things. Five appraisal checks are each valenced (pleasantness, goal conduciveness, power, self-congruence, moral goodness), and these "micro-valences" are integrated, by weighted sums or by lexicographic and elimination rules, into a one-dimensional "macro-valence" that serves as the common currency for choice. It separates intrinsic pleasantness from goal conduciveness and grounds the split in Berridge. It bears directly on the objection that the record's potential account tracks 'wanting', not 'liking' ([CLAIM-438](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-438.md)). |
| [LIT-1459](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1459.md) | Pleasure systems in the brain | Berridge & Kringelbach (2015), Neuron 86(3):646–664. Reward is three separable components: 'liking' (hedonic impact), 'wanting' (incentive salience) and learning. 'Liking' can be measured without report, by orofacial taste reactivity, which is homologous from rats to human infants. It is generated by cubic-millimetre opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots in nucleus accumbens, ventral pallidum and perhaps cortex and pons. Mesolimbic dopamine and most "pleasure electrodes" raise 'wanting' without raising 'liking'. Incentive sensitization makes an addict want a drug that has become less pleasant. Objective 'liking' can occur without any felt pleasure. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1110](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1110.md)): in full, from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC4425246, NIHMS664561). A review of the affective neuroscience of pleasure. Reward splits into 'liking' (hedonic impact), 'wanting' (incentive salience) and learning, with separable mechanisms. 'Liking' is measured without report by taste reactivity, which is homologous across rats, apes and newborn humans. It is generated by small opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots. Mesolimbic dopamine and most "pleasure electrodes" raise 'wanting' without raising 'liking'. Objective 'liking' can occur without felt pleasure. Filed for the record's account of valence as potential ([CLAIM-440](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-440.md)), which wanting-without-liking puts under pressure. |
| [LIT-1461](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1461.md) | Liking, wanting, and the incentive-sensitization theory of addiction | Berridge & Robinson (2016), American Psychologist 71(8):670–679. 'Wanting' (incentive salience, mesolimbic and dopamine-related) and 'liking' (hedonic impact, small opioid and endocannabinoid hotspots) are dissociable. Repeated, especially intermittent high-dose, drug use can sensitize the 'wanting' system, making it hyper-reactive to drug cues and contexts, lastingly and perhaps permanently, while 'liking' need not rise and may fall. Sensitized 'wanting' can oppose cognitive desire, run without report, and grow during abstinence. Its scope is said to extend, on emerging evidence, to behavioural addictions and to the compulsions of dopamine dysregulation syndrome. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1109](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1109.md)): in full, from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central (PMC5171207, NIHMS816820). Worth reading as the authors' own short statement, a quarter-century on, of the incentive-sensitization theory of addiction. Drugs, and perhaps unpredictable non-drug rewards, can make mesolimbic 'wanting' systems lastingly hyper-reactive to cues and contexts, and 'liking' need not rise with it. Sensitized 'wanting' can oppose a person's cognitive desire, operate without report, persist for years and grow during abstinence. It is a review of the authors' programme. Filed for the record's question whether potential of a proxy for maintenance is valence, and the form addiction and metric fixation share ([QUESTION-267](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-267.md)), to which it gives a mechanism on the personal side. |
| [LIT-1465](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1465.md) | A taxonomy of technology design features that promote potentially addictive online behaviours | Flayelle, Brevers, King, Maurage, Perales & Billieux (2023), Nature Reviews Psychology 2(3):136–150. Reviews evidence linking design features to loss of control in online gaming, gambling, cybersexual activity, shopping, social networking and streaming. Proposes a taxonomy based on model-free and model-based learning and control. Model-free: reinforcement schedules (random-ratio rewards such as loot boxes and likes) and personalized triggers (push notifications, recommendations). Model-based: overvaluation of outcomes, features that interfere with deliberation (autoplay, countdowns), partial goal fulfilment (infinite scroll, levels, progress bars) and features that strengthen cognitive biases (near-misses, losses disguised as wins). Providers keep whatever raises use or revenue, and informational asymmetry lets them personalize it. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1096](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1096.md)): in full, from the typeset article as deposited in the University of Lausanne's repository (SERVAL/IRIS). Worth reading as a compact, theory-driven catalogue of the design features of games, gambling, pornography, shopping, social-networking and streaming services that may weaken users' control. Features are sorted by whether they work on model-free learning (reinforcement schedules, personalized cues) or on model-based choice (overvaluation, features that interfere with deliberation, partial goal fulfilment, cognitive biases). It also names the selection process on the provider's side: features that raise use, time-on-device or spending are kept, with no psychology needed. The evidence reviewed is mostly cross-sectional, qualitative or indirect, and the authors warn against pathologizing common behaviour. Filed for the record's question whether potential of a proxy is valence ([QUESTION-267](../../../record/questions.d/QUESTION-267.md)), because it describes how a firm optimizing its own metric can install proxy-keyed potential in its users. |

Bumblebees chose between two 40% sucrose feeders, heated to 55 °C in the test phase, and two unheated alternatives of 10–40%. They avoided the heated feeders when the alternatives were also rich and fed from them more as the alternatives got poorer, guided by learned colour cues. The authors read this as a centrally mediated motivational trade-off, consistent with a capacity for pain. Corrected in 2025 for a misreported model. | Active — read 2026-10-23 ([NOTE-1114](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1114.md)): in full, from the published version (CC BY 4.0) in LSE Research Online, with the 2025 correction and the authors' deposited data. Worth reading as the cleanest published motivational trade-off in an insect. Bees chose between heated (55 °C) and unheated feeders. At this one cost the data are graded, not thresholded, and the design varies only the resource, so it cannot show a threshold in cost. |

| [LIT-1488](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1488.md) v2 | The when and how of planning: Meta-analysis of the scope and components of implementation intentions in 642 tests | Sheeran, Listrom & Gollwitzer (2024). Across 642 independent tests, forming implementation intentions was effective for cognitive, affective and behavioural outcomes (.27 ≤ d ≤ .66). Effects were larger when plans had a contingent if-then format, participants were highly motivated to reach the goal, and plans were rehearsed. A new taxonomy of the cues and responses that plans specify is developed and its categories tested. The effect is reliable (BF10 = 319) but small once publication bias is modelled (d = .15, against an uncorrected .36 and 2006's .65), and highly heterogeneous. Between tests, the conditional link beats a schedule of the same behaviour, rehearsal helps, keeping a copy to revisit hurts, and plans work only when the goal is wanted. Its taxonomy finds nearly every cue and response effective, ignoring and waiting before responding among them. No mechanism is tested. |

| [LIT-1689](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1689.md) | The Concept and Psychological Consequences of Symbolic Immortality | An ANU master's thesis in psychology testing Otto Rank's idea that people need to feel they will transcend death, in three modes (children, an afterlife, creative work), to which Lifton added two (nature and experiential transcendence, an expansion of the self). It reviews ethnographic, ancient and modern evidence that all five modes are expressed. Then it surveys 440 Australian adults aged 18 to 88, recruited through Christian, Yoga, Spiritualist and secular groups, using vignettes rated as imagined consolation in terminal illness. Having a mode in one's life and religious affiliation predict accepting it; education predicts accepting the modes less. The modes predict personality only weakly; Rank's links to neuroticism and to sex differences fail. | Active — skimmed 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1312](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1312.md)), in place of [LIT-1714](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1714.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as a review of how Rank's and Lifton's modes were measured by 1991, and as one survey showing that the secular modes go with accepting death as final. It is a modest test that found little; skim chapters 1, 4 and 10. |
| [LIT-1691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1691.md) | Generativity as a Route to Active Ageing | A gerontological essay with a report of the authors' own studies. It reads Erikson's generativity, as McAdams models it, as the psychological form of an ethical category of "joint responsibility", and argues it is a lifelong concern, not a midlife task. It restates McAdams' model: generativity springs from cultural demand and from an inner desire made of a "need to be needed" and a need for symbolic immortality, and passes through concern, commitment and belief in the species to action and a life-story script. It distinguishes generativity from altruism and says generative engagement can be selfish or altruistic in motive. Studies of 3,308 people aged 59 to 108 in Mexico, Spain and Germany found generativity predicted optimism and life satisfaction beyond health, money and family status. An intervention of intergenerational dialogue projects in Belarus, Russia and Ukraine raised Loyola Generativity Scale scores in old and young participants. No test statistics are reported. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1261](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1261.md)), in place of [LIT-1777](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1777.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as a compact restatement of McAdams' model of generativity, with symbolic immortality as one of its motives, and for its claim that generativity serves the well-being of the old. |
| [LIT-1693](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1693.md) | Psychometric validation of the Loyola Generativity Scale in Chilean teachers: evidence for a three factor structure | A validation of McAdams and de St. Aubin's 20-item Loyola Generativity Scale (LGS) in Spanish, with 430 Chilean elementary teachers. Four items were dropped for low sampling adequacy, and a three-factor solution on 14 items was retained (RMSEA = 0.043, CFI = 0.989): Generative Inefficacy (three reverse-scored items), Generative Action (eight items on teaching, creativity and community work) and Generative Legacy (three items on symbolic continuity and contribution to future generations). Action and Legacy correlated .45; Inefficacy correlated −.34 and −.30 with them. Factor-score reliabilities were .80 to .86. The authors read the three factors as an extension of the original two (positive generativity and generative doubts) produced by the teaching context. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1260](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1260.md)), in place of [LIT-1777](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1777.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as evidence that legacy motivation can be measured apart from generative action within McAdams' scale, with the caution that the analysis is exploratory and two items vanish unexplained. |
| [LIT-1702](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1702.md) | Future self-continuity: how conceptions of the future self transform intertemporal choice | Hershfield (2011). A review, mostly of the author's own studies, of "future self-continuity": following Parfit, people who feel their future self is less connected to them treat it more like a stranger and save less for it. Three components are proposed. Similarity, measured by choosing overlapping circles (adapted from Aron et al.'s inclusion-of-other-in-self scale) for one's self in ten years, predicted patient choices and accumulated assets, controlling for age; neural activity for the future self that looked more like activity for another person predicted steeper discounting (r = .47). Vividness: seeing an age-progressed image of oneself raised hypothetical retirement saving. Positivity: respect for the elderly tracked national saving rates and, when induced, raised patient choices. Asking directly how much people liked and cared for their future selves did not predict choice, though those answers were near ceiling. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1259](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1259.md)) from the NIH author manuscript (PMC3764505), served by NCBI's PMC OAI-PMH service after Europe PMC refused this client; worth reading as the short statement of the future self-continuity programme, and as the record's clearest case of a measured extent of the self predicting concern-like behaviour where directly reported caring did not. Read it knowing that the review gives almost no statistics, that the caring null comes from a ceiling, and that the circles are framed as similarity. |
| [LIT-1713](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1713.md) | Responsibility to Future Generations: A Moral Reframing Strategy for Combatting Climate Change | Syropoulos, Kraft-Todd, Mah, Markowitz & Young (2023). Thirteen studies (six main, seven supplementary; N = 161,633) on felt responsibility to future generations (RFG). In Eurobarometer data from 34 European countries (N = 109,513), a majority in 33 agreed "We need to reform to benefit future generations even if that means making some sacrifices now"; agreement barely related to ideology, age or gender (meta-r .03 to .07) and weakly to subjective status (.13). In US samples RFG was endorsed more than responsibility to reduce one's own contribution to climate change (RCC), correlated with conservatism half as strongly (meta-r −.21 against −.45), and predicted self-reported proenvironmental behaviour, concern and policy support. In a preregistered experiment (N = 3,175), five brief interventions (a letter to a person born today, legacy reflection, reflection on past generations' sacrifices, a park video, a 385-word excerpt of *What We Owe the Future*) each raised RFG and proenvironmental intentions by small amounts (d = .14 to .54); only the letter raised donations. Reflection on past sacrifices raised RFG but not RCC. All outcomes are self-reports or a small donation. **status_note**: worth reading as the largest study of felt responsibility to future generations, its spread and its political neutrality, and as the record's only experiment comparing legacy, reciprocity, a particular future person and an impersonal longtermist text as routes to it; read in place of Syropoulos and Markowitz 2021. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1293](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1293.md)), in place of [LIT-1741](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1741.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the largest study of felt responsibility to future generations, its spread and its political neutrality, and as the record's only experiment comparing legacy, reciprocity, a particular future person and an impersonal longtermist text as routes to it; read in place of Syropoulos and Markowitz 2021. |
| [LIT-1714](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1714.md) | The Broken Connection: On Death and the Continuity of Life | Lifton (1979). A psychiatric account of "symbolic immortality": a sense of continuity with what came before and what will come after, sought in five modes, biological (living on through one's children and people), creative (one's works and influence), theological, natural, and experiential transcendence. Its loss underlies much of the psychopathology of death. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher. The Internet Archive holds it only as a lending item; Lifton's own 1973 restatement is closed. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Sturesteps 1992 ([LIT-1689](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1689.md)). |
| [LIT-1716](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1716.md) | Legacies, Immortality, and the Future: The Psychology of Intergenerational Altruism | Wade-Benzoni (2006). Argues that intergenerational beneficence, sacrifice now for people who will live later and cannot reciprocate, is motivated in part by the desire to leave a legacy, a route to symbolic immortality, and that this motive can be engaged to promote decisions that favour future generations. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher; Scholars@Duke and Duke's faculty pages list it without a file. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Wade-Benzoni, Sondak and Galinsky 2010 ([LIT-1717](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1717.md)). |
| [LIT-1717](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1717.md) | Leaving a Legacy: Intergenerational Allocations of Benefits and Burdens | Six experiments (N = 76, 101, 64, 32, 131, 92; U.S. undergraduates, MBA students and university staff) on how the valence of what is passed on affects concern for one's legacy and generosity to future others. Framing climate change as leaving burdens, rather than using up benefits, raised a generativity scale built from items about being remembered and living on (4.90 vs 4.10), direct concern with one's legacy, felt responsibility and affinity toward future generations, and ethical concern; recalling one's own past burden allocation raised moral emotions. In allocation tasks people favoured themselves more with benefits than with burdens. The difference appeared only when the recipient was in the future (not in a dictator-game version with a present recipient), and only when the allocator was a party to the trade-off (not when allocating between two other people). One item on ethical considerations statistically accounted for the first of these. The authors read the pattern as legacy concern, which they define as the wish to extend the self beyond death, engaged more by leaving burdens than by withholding benefits. Legacy concern was measured only in the attitude studies, never in the allocation studies. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1273](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1273.md)), in place of [LIT-1716](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1716.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the legacy programme's fullest experimental statement before the 2012 mortality studies, and as the record's only second-hand source for Wade-Benzoni 2006 ([LIT-1716](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1716.md)). Read it knowing that legacy concern and generosity are never measured in the same study, and that the generosity effects sit in one cell: people keep more benefits for themselves when the other person will receive them later. |
| [LIT-1719](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1719.md) | I Belong, therefore, I Exist: Ingroup Identification, Ingroup Entitativity, and Ingroup Bias | Castano, Yzerbyt, Paladino & Sacchi (2002). One experiment with 48 Italian students. Those who wrote about the emotions their own death aroused, rather than about reading a book, then identified more with Italians (6.19 vs 5.09), saw Italians as more of an entity (5.40 vs 4.77) and showed more in-group bias against Germans (1.01 vs 0.45), the last entirely through rating Italians higher. Identification and entitativity, which a factor analysis separates (r = .59), each mediated the effect on bias, through what they share. The authors propose, without testing it, that a group seen as a real, lasting entity lets people project themselves beyond their own death; the standard reading, defence of a worldview the group shares, is not ruled out. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1297](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1297.md)) from the published version on co-author Yzerbyt's UCLouvain page; worth reading as the study that joins terror management to social identity, and as the clearest statement of the idea that a group seen as a lasting entity lets the self outlive death. Read it knowing that it is one small study of an effect, mortality salience, whose replicability is now in question, and that it does not test its own proposal against the worldview-defence reading. |
| [LIT-1724](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1724.md) | How Will I Be Remembered? Conserving the Environment for the Sake of One's Legacy | Zaval, Markowitz & Weber (2015). Legacy motivation, wanting to be remembered well, predicted pro-environmental intentions and donations, and writing about how one wants to be remembered increased donations to an environmental charity and pro-environmental intentions. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher. A PDF on the Wharton marketing department's site was not used, since none of the authors is there; the authors' own deposits at Columbia Academic Commons hold the study materials and data, not the article. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Wickersham et al. 2020 (LIT-1750). |
| [LIT-1730](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1730.md) | Managing the Terror of Publication Bias: A Systematic Review of the Mortality Salience Hypothesis | A systematic review of the mortality-salience (MS) hypothesis of terror management theory, that reminders of death increase worldview defense. An uncorrected random-effects meta-analysis of 635 effects reproduces Burke et al.'s (2010) moderate effect (g = 0.81, about r = .37, against their r = .35 over 277 studies), but a funnel plot shows strong asymmetry. Bias corrections disagree. Selection models and WAAP-WLS give a small effect, about r = .18; PET-PEESE finds none. A p-curve of 825 focal tests shows that some studies test real effects, at an average power of 25%; z-curve gives an expected replication rate of 19% and an expected discovery rate of 8%, near the 5% of a literature of null effects. Five of nine preregistered replications succeeded, and Many Labs 4 did not. The authors conclude the literature holds some non-zero effects, much smaller and far more heterogeneous than published, and that most studies are underpowered. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1271](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1271.md)), in place of [LIT-1687](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1687.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the current quantitative verdict on the mortality-salience hypothesis, and as the only source the record holds for Burke et al.'s figures. |
| [LIT-1737](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1737.md) | Evolution, altruism and cognitive architecture: a critique of Sober and Wilson's argument for psychological altruism | Stich (2006/2007). Restates Sober and Wilson's argument that natural selection is unlikely to have made us pure egoists: for parental care, an ultimate desire for the child's welfare is a more reliable mechanism than hedonism, which depends on beliefs linking helping to one's own pleasure and pain. Stich rejects three of their four arguments outright. The fourth, that hedonism's linking beliefs could be undermined by evidence, fails if the links are sticky sub-doxastic states. So the argument leaves egoism open; it does not show it true. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1282](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1282.md)) from the published version on Stich's own site; worth reading as a close restatement and critique of Sober and Wilson's evolutionary argument for psychological altruism, read in place of Unto Others ([LIT-1683](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1683.md), Unavailable), and for its definitions of egoism, altruism and ultimate desire, which the owner's thesis ([CLAIM-491](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-491.md)) has to meet. |
| [LIT-1741](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1741.md) | Perceived responsibility towards future generations and environmental concern: Convergent evidence across multiple outcomes in a large, nationally representative sample | Syropoulos & Markowitz (2021). In a large, nationally representative US sample, perceived responsibility towards future generations predicted environmental concern and pro-environmental intentions across several outcomes, beyond demographics and political ideology. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher; it is Elsevier subscription content, and OSF holds no preprint of it. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Syropoulos et al.'s 2023 preprint (LIT-1713). |
| [LIT-1750](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1750.md) | The impact of place and legacy framing on climate action: A lifespan approach | Wickersham et al. (2020). An online experiment with 988 American adults aged 18 to 87, sampled evenly by age. Writing about what one wants future generations to remember one for (adapted from Zaval et al. 2015), or about a beloved place and climate change, raised pro-environmental intentions (η² = .030) and hypothetical donations to a tree-planting charity (η² = .009) against a scrambled-eggs control. Age did not moderate either effect. The legacy writing raised scores on an eight-item Legacy Motivation Scale, which statistically mediated part of its effect; but the place writing raised legacy motivation too, the legacy writing raised love of nature, and in a model with both mediators love of nature carried as much of the donation effect. The scale mixes wanting to be remembered with self-regard and felt responsibility to future generations, so the study does not show that wanting to be remembered is what moves people. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1316](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1316.md)), in place of [LIT-1724](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1724.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the one open use of Zaval et al.'s legacy induction and Legacy Motivation Scale, with the scale's items in print; it shows the scale bundles the wish to be remembered with caring about future generations. |
| [LIT-1760](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1760.md) | It's Only a Matter of Time: Death, Legacies, and Intergenerational Decisions | Wade-Benzoni, Tost, Hernandez & Larrick (2012). In experiments, reminders of death increased people's allocations of resources to future generations, an effect the authors attribute to the desire to leave a positive legacy. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher; Scholars@Duke and the co-authors' Duke pages list it without a file. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Hurlstone et al. 2020 ([LIT-1785](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1785.md)). |
| [LIT-1771](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1771.md) | Social Influence and Group Identity | A review, by one of the SIDE model's authors, of the self-categorization account of social influence. Group influence is not only compliance for approval (normative influence). Because a group can be a level of the self, influence from in-group members can be true private acceptance ("referent informational influence"). Classic findings are reread this way: Asch and Sherif conformity, Milgram obedience, minority influence, emergency crowds, bystander helping, emotional contagion and riots. Influence is moderated by identification, prototypicality, intergroup threat and context. Isolation and visual anonymity strengthen group influence rather than weakening it, as the SIDE model predicts. Crowd members do not lose the self; they switch to a group identity. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1268](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1268.md)), in place of [LIT-1726](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1726.md) and [LIT-1731](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1731.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the most recent overview, by an author of the SIDE model, of how self-categorization theory treats influence, norms and deindividuation, and as the record's second-hand access to Postmes & Spears 1998. |
| [LIT-1772](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1772.md) | Social identity theory | A textbook chapter. Social identity is "that part of an individual's self-concept which derives from knowledge of membership in a social group (or groups) together with the value or emotional significance attached to that membership" (Tajfel 1978). The theory has two parts. In the first, categorization is always self-relevant, and the motive for a positive social identity drives comparison with out-groups. That identity serves needs for certainty, self-esteem and meaning. In the second, members of low-status groups choose individual mobility, collective action or social creativity, depending on the permeability of group boundaries and the legitimacy and stability of status differences. Identification has cognitive, affective and behavioural components. Applications: identification improves health behaviour and buffers stress; at work it matters more than instrumental interdependence and motivates volunteers. An imagined common in-group raised Italian children's willingness to help an immigrant classmate. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1315](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1315.md)), in place of [LIT-1695](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1695.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as a current statement of social identity theory by two of its principal researchers, read in place of Tajfel & Turner 1979 ([LIT-1695](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1695.md), Unavailable). It is the record's clearest source that the theory builds caring into the definition of social identity while measuring it as a separate component. Uncritical, with no effect sizes. |
| [LIT-1777](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1777.md) | A theory of generativity and its assessment through self-report, behavioral acts, and narrative themes in autobiography | McAdams & de St. Aubin (1992). Models Erikson's generativity, concern for and commitment to the next generation, as seven features: cultural demand, inner desire (for symbolic immortality and to be needed), concern, belief in the species, commitment, action and narration. Introduces the Loyola Generativity Scale and a checklist of generative acts, with evidence from adult samples and autobiographies. | Unavailable — filed 2026-10-29; reading attempted the same day, no lawful copy reached. Unpaywall lists no open copy and a web search found none posted by an author, their institution or the publisher; a summary on a Notre Dame page was unreachable, Northwestern's Foley Center pages return 404, and copies on Scribd and a commercial site were not used. No NOTE is filed. It stays Unavailable until a copy is supplied ([ADR-041](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-041.md)). Read in its place, and not a substitute for reading it: Kruse and Schmitt 2012 ([LIT-1691](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1691.md)) and Sandoval-Obando et al. 2026 ([LIT-1693](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1693.md)). |
| [LIT-1779](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1779.md) | The Afterlife (Tanner Lectures I and II) | Scheffler's 2012 Tanner Lectures, the source of the first two chapters of *Death and the Afterlife*. By "the afterlife" he means that other people will live on after one's own death. Imagined reactions to a doomsday scenario (the earth destroyed thirty days after one's death) and to P. D. James's infertility scenario (no one dies early, but no one more is born) show that this matters to us in its own right and as a condition of other things mattering. Without it many projects, and perhaps even reading and eating well, would lose their point (the "afterlife conjecture"). So, in one respect, humanity's survival matters more to us than our own or our loved ones'. Scheffler reads this as dependence on future people, not as unsuspected altruism toward them, and as showing that individual valuing presupposes humanity as an ongoing historical project. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1298](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1298.md)), in place of [LIT-1754](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1754.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the exact statement of the afterlife conjecture and of what Scheffler does and does not infer from it: our dependence on future people, not altruism toward them. The third essay, the commentaries and the replies are in the book only. |
| [LIT-1785](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1785.md) | Activating the legacy motive mitigates intergenerational discounting in the climate game | A laboratory climate game: 180 people in 30 groups of six, each with $40 to spend, decide over ten rounds whether to put $0, $2 or $4 into a climate account. If the group reaches $120, each member's $45 endowment is saved; if not, it is lost with 90% probability. When the saved endowments were paid to the players the next day, 9 of 10 groups reached the target. When they went instead to planting trees for future generations, 2 of 10 did. When players in the tree-planting game also read three short messages meant to activate the legacy motive (death awareness, the powerlessness of future generations, and paying forward a past generation's sacrifice), 7 of 10 did, and group investment rose from $77.20 to $105.20. All three messages raised investment over the matched rounds of the plain tree-planting game. Legacy induction made fair shares, not extra giving, the norm. There were no manipulation checks and no control message. The authors say people invest in legacies "for largely—although not entirely—selfish reasons". | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1279](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1279.md)), in place of [LIT-1760](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1760.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as a conceptual extension of the 2012 mortality-and-legacy result to group cooperation, and as the record's nearest substitute for Wade-Benzoni et al. 2012 ([LIT-1760](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1760.md)). Read it knowing that its legacy induction bundles three mechanisms, one of them identification with past and future generations, so it cannot say which did the work. |
| [LIT-1796](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1796.md) | Many Labs 4: Failure to Replicate Mortality Salience Effect With and Without Original Author Involvement | A preregistered multisite replication of Study 1 of Greenberg et al. (1994), the standard mortality-salience test: writing about one's own death, against writing about watching television, was to raise preference for a pro-US over an anti-US essay author. Seventeen US university labs contributed 1,550 usable participants. Seven ran a protocol designed with the original authors; ten built their own. The pooled effect was Hedges' g = 0.07 (95% CI −0.03 to 0.17), against the original d = 1.34, and no exclusion rule, protocol type or subset of TMT-knowledgeable labs produced a significant effect. Effects did not vary across labs more than chance allows, so the test of whether expert involvement helps replication was left without an effect to act on. | Active — read in full 2026-10-29 ([NOTE-1322](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1322.md)), in place of [LIT-1687](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1687.md), which could not be reached; worth reading as the best-powered direct test of terror management theory's worldview-defense prediction, and as the fullest record of how its original authors think the effect must be produced. |
